items.title: In London, there are at least two people with exactly the same number of hairs
items.claim: Humans have at most about 150,000 hairs on their heads. London has over 9 million people. By the pigeonhole principle, at least 60 Londoners share an EXACT hair count.

options.text: If you put more than n items into n containers, at least one container has at least 2 items; more generally, if k*n + 1 items go into n containers, some container has at least k + 1

items.reveal:
The pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's drawer principle, 1834): if you put n + 1 objects into n boxes, at least one box has at least 2 objects.

Applied to London: ~9 million heads, at most ~150,000 possible hair counts. 9 million divided by 150,000 = 60. So at least 60 Londoners share a hair count exactly.

Elegant applications:
- In any group of 367 people, two share a birthday (366 possible birthdays + leap year).
- Among any 6 people, three are mutual friends or three mutual strangers (a Ramsey theory result, R(3,3) = 6).
- Among any 10 distinct integers from 1 to 100, two have a sum or difference divisible by 17.
- In any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct real numbers, there is a monotone subsequence of length n+1 (Erdős-Szekeres).

The principle gives existence proofs without constructing the example. It's surprisingly powerful for such a simple idea.
items.why: The pigeonhole principle looks obvious but yields non-trivial results — existence guarantees from pure counting, often where direct construction is hopeless.

items.title: A note in a margin that took 358 years to verify
items.claim: Pierre de Fermat wrote in 1637 that he had a proof — too long for the margin — that a to the n + b to the n equals c to the n has no positive-integer solutions for n greater than 2. Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
items.prompt: Why was Fermat's Last Theorem so hard to prove?

options.text: Fermat lied about having a proof — there isn't one

It was eventually shown to be equivalent to a statement about modular forms and elliptic curves (the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture); the modern proof required machinery that didn't exist until the 1980s
Number theorists weren't trying hard enough
It is undecidable in standard axioms

items.reveal_title: Wiles, Frey, Ribet — a chain of insights
items.reveal:
Fermat wrote his marginal note in Diophantus's Arithmetica. Hundreds of mathematicians attempted the proof. Special cases were handled (n = 4 by Fermat himself; n = 3 by Euler; n = 5, 7 in the 1800s).

In 1985, Frey proposed that any non-trivial solution would correspond to an unusual elliptic curve. In 1986, Ribet proved this curve could not be 'modular'. Combined with the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture (all elliptic curves are modular), no solution could exist.

Wiles worked in secret for seven years on Taniyama-Shimura for a key class of elliptic curves. He announced the proof in 1993. A gap was found. With Richard Taylor he repaired it in late 1994. The proof runs over 100 pages and uses 20th-century algebraic geometry that Fermat couldn't have had.

It's almost certain Fermat did not have a real proof. He probably had a flawed attempt for small cases, since he never mentioned the result in subsequent letters.
items.why: Fermat's Last Theorem feels like an elementary statement about integers. Its proof needed centuries of machinery — number theory, algebraic geometry, automorphic forms — that no one in 1637 could have imagined.

items.title: A shape whose boundary has infinite length but encloses finite area
items.claim: The Mandelbrot set is the set of complex numbers c such that iterating z to z squared plus c starting from 0 stays bounded. Its area is about 1.5 square units. Its boundary has infinite length and Hausdorff dimension 2.
items.prompt: How can the boundary have infinite length but enclose finite area?

options.text: Modern computers can't measure it accurately
Fractal boundaries are not 1-dimensional curves; they have intrinsic 'roughness' that produces infinite arclength while still enclosing finite area — the boundary's Hausdorff dimension is 2
The boundary contains infinitely many smaller boundaries

items.reveal:
The Mandelbrot set was first plotted by Brooks and Matelski in 1978, then explored extensively by Mandelbrot in 1980. Zoom into any boundary region and you find copies of the original set repeated at smaller scales — true self-similarity.

A smooth curve (like a circle) has dimension 1 and finite length per unit area. A jagged curve with detail at every scale can have a 'dimension' between 1 and 2, and infinite length per unit area. Hausdorff dimension formalises this.

The Mandelbrot boundary's Hausdorff dimension is exactly 2 (Shishikura, 1998). Despite this, the set has finite, computable area (about 1.506 square units, though no closed form is known).

This kind of geometry shows up in nature — coastlines, lungs, river networks, cauliflower. Mandelbrot's 1983 book The Fractal Geometry of Nature popularised the term and the field.
items.why: Length and area are usually proportional in geometry. Fractals decouple them — finite area, infinite perimeter — and this is not an artefact but a real measurable property.
